extracted.intended_audience: prospective middle grades teachers and college mathematics instructors (teacher-educators)
extracted.subtask_short: designing math content course for teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and standards for designing and assessing undergraduate activity-based mathematics content courses (algebra; probability & statistics) for prospective middle grades teachers, including class activities, readings, homework, quizzes, projects, and exams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class Activity design
rubrics_metrics.description: Class Activities are intended to motivate new topics. They must have a rich mathematical content, but be accessible before a formal introduction to the ideas. The problems should be open to multiple problem-solving strategies. We begin each week with a new class activity. Students work in small groups toward a solution. We expect the work and the discussions to require a one-hour class period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide materials and an instructor’s guide indicating objectives and a line of questioning. After group work, hold a whole-class discussion to elicit notation and definitions and to raise natural follow-up questions (e.g., robustness to outliers, scaling to other problems). Examples: the M&M jar estimation activity. Instructor skill and preparation strongly affect the value of discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and Study design
rubrics_metrics.description: Each Class Activity is followed by a Read and Study section that is usually short—typically two pages—and is meant to be read slowly and carefully, with pencil in hand. The sections do not include worked examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include questions written in italics that students must attempt (not rhetorical). Encourage students to verify claims and answer italicized questions while reading. Use history and context to show mathematics as a human endeavor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connections to the middle grades curriculum
rubrics_metrics.description: Connections sections are designed to show students how the ideas they are studying are treated in the middle grades curriculum. The sections often include pages from children’s texts, and are followed by questions or homework that asks students to relate the content to ideas in the Read and Study section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete classroom examples (e.g., tower/cube illustrations of the mean) and ask students to adapt classroom-level explanations for middle school students. Classroom discussion of these connections is important and built into course structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homework design
rubrics_metrics.description: Homework sets are thorough but do not repeat concepts. Each set consists of questions that have students apply concepts and generalize concepts from the section. Homework problems (usually five to ten) are assigned on completion of the readings for each section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems should be non-routine and foundational (not mimicking textbook solutions). Many problems should be substantial enough to serve as topics for student presentations. Classes meet frequently to allow discussion of homework in class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homework assessment criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: We assign and grade almost all the homework. Students are assessed on the accuracy and explanation of their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective student solutions include appropriate sketches, are focused on conceptual understanding instead of rote rule use, and are often written so that an upper elementary or middle school student can understand the explanation. Homework can be assessed via collected written solutions, exam questions, or presentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quizzes and written exams
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular, short written quizzes are effective while using these materials. Depending on the course structure, a one-question quiz to start each day, or a two- or three-question quiz each week may be best. We prefer to use written chapter exams in our courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To encourage cooperative learning, it is possible to allow groups to discuss the exam (usually without writing) for five minutes before students individually write out their exam solutions. Short, regular quizzes should test application and understanding rather than rote repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral final exam format
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an oral final exam. A 20 to 25 minute session with each student (with a five minute break between students) is ideal. We have a list of questions ready to ask and a sorted set of algebra pieces ready to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pages for pattern and sequence analysis and have students sketch graphs. Oral finals are cumulative and allow students who struggled with written work to demonstrate understanding. Keep a set of notes for each student during the exam, with scores for each question; although scheduling is time-consuming, final grading is usually quick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment tools mix
rubrics_metrics.description: The typical assessment tools (homework, quizzes, and exams) are used in this course, and there is an oral final exam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine multiple assessment modes to see different facets of student understanding (written, collaborative, oral). Use cumulative and formative assessments to support conceptual mastery and teaching-focused outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class participation and attendance
rubrics_metrics.description: Active participation is required and is built into our grading policy, along with class attendance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect students to prepare Read and Study sections before class so they can contribute meaningfully to activities and discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor’s guide purpose and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: We have prepared a guide for instructors. It is not a solutions manual, nor does it provide information that would be shared with students. Its use is to provide technical guidance so that student discussions may be appropriately directed by the instructor and to provide insight as to why we wrote the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include objectives, suggested lines of questioning, and commentary on common student approaches and misconceptions. Provide suggested numerical answers or approaches where appropriate (e.g., assigning 1 for head and 0 for tail to connect proportion and mean).

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem design principles (Read/Study/Homework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems are designed to expand upon readings and connections; they are never routine exercises. Students are expected to work through problems rather than mimic solutions. Problems often force students to confront misconceptions and make careful modeling choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include open-ended or context-rich problems (e.g., evaluating whether two deaths at a movie are unusual) and encourage debate about merits/weaknesses of approaches. Include frequent cautionary remarks about pitfalls of blindly applying statistical methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group project requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Group projects vary by instructor and can deal with probability, statistics, their history, or educational issues. Students are asked to work outside of class on these projects in groups of 2–4, and sometimes to present their results in class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One example project: complete a statistical study—choose a population and research question, design a survey or data collection method, gather data under numerical and categorical variables, analyze using regression, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, and write a paper summarizing findings; present results in class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of manipulatives and progression to symbolic methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Due to limitations of algebra pieces, students initially focus on using algebra pieces and symbolic work to solve one-variable linear equations with integer coefficients and constants. After students become comfortable, they determine steps needed to solve all one-variable linear equations including those with rational coefficients and constants. Similarly, algebra pieces are used to model quadratic expressions and factorization visually before teaching algebraic methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start concrete (white strips, variable squares, tiles) and connect numerical, verbal, symbolic, and graphical representations. Teach visual factoring (factor rectangles, edge-sets) and then introduce algebraic methods such as the ac-method to reinforce connections. Note special visual rules: if a and c have same sign, visual factoring may not need extra zero pairs; if opposite sign, add equal numbers of white and opposite white strips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity deliverables for tile-sequence/quadratic analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: For a tile-sequence activity, students should analyze an extended sequence, give the symbolic formula simplified into y = ax^2 + bx + c form and sketch the xth figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should identify constant term (y-intercept), linear growth (b), quadratic growth (a, via red square arrays), find y-intercept, x-intercepts, turning point, range, and factored form (both algebraically and with algebra pieces). They should sketch models and graph the quadratic and show full work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral exam scoring and record-keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: During oral exams instructors keep a set of notes for each student, with scores for each question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a sorted set of manipulatives and prepared pages; schedule 20–25 minute slots with short breaks. While scheduling is time-consuming, summarizing and recording interview notes makes final grading quick.
